# Getting Started with C++ Using a Maintenance Project Approach

## Prologue

If you approach learning C++ using conventional methods—that is, by first familiarizing yourself with the official syntax documentation—you'll find the sheer volume of syntax overwhelming. Keywords appear endlessly, and sometimes you're left unsure how to even begin writing a program. The syntax feels highly abstract, like this:

```cpp
// This code is generated by the Gemini-3 Flash large language model.
#include <iostream>

template<int N>
struct AbstractLogic {
    static constexpr unsigned long value = 
        AbstractLogic<N - 1>::value + AbstractLogic<N - 2>::value;
};

template<>
struct AbstractLogic<1> {
    static constexpr unsigned long value = 1;
};

template<>
struct AbstractLogic<0> {
    static constexpr unsigned long value = 0;
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "The 20th level of abstraction: " 
              << AbstractLogic<20>::value << std::endl;
    
    return 0;
}
```

The syntax of the standard library is so overwhelming it makes you question your existence. That's why this tutorial will take a different approach to introduce you to C++: by maintaining a project—specifically, by directly analyzing project source code to learn C++ syntax.

## How to Write C++ Programs

First, create a source file with the `test.cpp` extension. Then open it with Neovim. If you're unfamiliar with using Neovim as an editor, you can refer to my previous article or wait for my upcoming tutorial on Vim key bindings.

After opening this file, I'll assume you're already in insert mode. What you need to do next is write the following content:

```cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "hello world" << std::endl;
}
```

Why do you need to input this content? Because it forms the foundation required for a C++ program to run. Unlike languages like Lua where you can get by with just a few lines of code, the `main()` function here only executes after compilation. You can define a bunch of private functions, data types, and so on outside this function within the program.

If you need to compile and run the program, you must save the file and then return to the command line. Enter the following command:

```bash
g++ test.cpp -o test
```

This compiles the program into a binary file, enabling it to be executed.

## How to Learn C++ Through Maintaining Projects

The above outlines only the most fundamental steps for compiling C++ programs. Now comes the main topic: how to learn basic C++ syntax by maintaining projects. You can start by searching GitHub for open-source projects written in C++, such as Microsoft Terminal.

[pictures]

[Source Code Directory](https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/tree/main/src)

We discovered that the `src/` directory contains numerous pre-written tools. When you navigate into any tool's directory, you'll find it contains many pre-written programs.

Then when you open one of these files to analyze its source code, you'll find it's filled with keywords:

[Console Monitor](https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/blob/main/src/tools/ConsoleMonitor/main.cpp)

Several keywords appear frequently, such as: `static`, `const`, `bool`, `void`, `const`, `auto`, `for`, `case`, `default`, `int`, `try`, `catch`, `return`, and so on. These are the keywords we need to study. Among them, `const` denotes a constant, while `bool` represents a Boolean value, corresponding to two fixed values: true and false. `return` is used to return data, `int` represents an integer, and `for` is used to execute the same operation based on the quantity of data. It is typically paired with `void` to encapsulate it into a function for use. Here, `auto` is used for automatic type deduction of variables. `try` and `catch` are for exception handling. The `default` keyword is slightly more complex and will be covered in the next tutorial; we won't elaborate further here.
